name: The Milgram Experiment
statement: Ordinary people, ordered by an authority, kept delivering shocks they thought were harming a stranger.
statementAccent: kept delivering shocks they thought were harming a stranger
meaning: The Milgram experiment was a series of social-psychology studies on obedience to authority, conducted by the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram beginning in 1961. In each session, a participant, cast as a teacher, was ordered by an experimenter in a lab coat to administer what they believed were increasingly severe electric shocks to a learner, actually an actor who was not really shocked, each time the learner answered a memory question wrong. The shock generator was labelled up to 450 volts, marked as dangerous. Despite the learner's staged cries and pleas, a striking proportion of participants, about sixty-five percent in the baseline condition, continued all the way to the maximum voltage when prodded by the experimenter with phrases like the experiment requires that you continue. Milgram launched the study amid the trial of Adolf Eichmann and the question of how ordinary people could take part in Holocaust atrocities under orders. The experiment became one of the most famous and controversial in psychology, taken to demonstrate the power of authority, though it is now criticized on both ethical and methodological grounds.
mechanism: Each session involved three roles: the experimenter, the authority figure; the teacher, the actual naive participant; and the learner, a confederate. The teacher was told to shock the learner for each wrong answer, raising the voltage each time on a generator running up to 450 volts. The learner, in another room, gave scripted wrong answers and produced pre-recorded protests, screams, and eventually silence as the shocks supposedly intensified. When the teacher hesitated, the experimenter delivered a fixed sequence of prods, from please continue to the experiment requires that you continue to you have no other choice, you must go on. Milgram measured how far up the voltage scale participants would go. He had expected only a tiny fraction to reach the maximum, but about sixty-five percent of participants in the baseline condition continued to 450 volts. Milgram interpreted this through the idea of an agentic state, in which a person comes to see themselves as merely an instrument of the authority and displaces responsibility onto it. Obedience rates varied considerably across the many conditions he ran.

examples.text: About sixty-five percent of participants in the baseline condition continued to the maximum 450 volts despite the learner's staged screams and pleas.
When teachers hesitated, the experimenter used fixed prods like the experiment requires that you continue to press them onward.
Milgram began the study amid Adolf Eichmann's trial, probing how ordinary people could take part in atrocities under orders.

variants.name: The agentic state
variants.text: Milgram's idea that under authority a person sees themselves as an instrument carrying out orders, displacing personal responsibility.

variants.name: Varying conditions
variants.text: The many variants Milgram ran, such as changing proximity to the learner or the authority, which produced widely different obedience rates.

whyItMatters: The Milgram experiment is among the most famous and influential studies in the history of psychology, dramatizing how ordinary people can be led by authority to act against their conscience. Coming in the wake of the Holocaust and the Eichmann trial, its finding that a majority of ordinary participants would deliver seemingly lethal shocks under orders shocked the public and the profession, and it became a touchstone for thinking about obedience, conformity, and the situational forces that can drive atrocity, challenging the comforting belief that only monstrous people commit monstrous acts. The study also transformed research ethics: the deception and psychological distress it inflicted on participants helped spur the development of modern ethical standards and review boards for human research. At the same time, the experiment is now heavily scrutinized, with critics questioning its ethics, its interpretation, and the reliability of its archival record, so it stands as both a landmark and a cautionary tale. Its lasting importance lies in the uncomfortable question it raised about how far people will go when told to obey.

working.text: cast the participant as teacher, ordered by an experimenter to shock a learner who is secretly an actor.
have the teacher raise the voltage for each wrong answer, pressed on by the experimenter's fixed prods despite the learner's protests.
record how far up the scale participants go, finding many continue to the maximum, and interpret this as obedience to authority.

limits: The Milgram experiment is ethically controversial by modern standards, since it deceived participants and subjected them to real psychological distress without adequate consent or debriefing, and such a study could not be run today. Its interpretation is also debated: obedience rates varied widely across the more than twenty conditions rather than sitting at a single sixty-five percent, and archival research, notably by Gina Perry, has argued that only about half of participants fully believed the shocks were real, that experimenters sometimes went off the fixed script, and that results may have been presented selectively. The sample was limited, and generalizing from a lab to real atrocities is contested.
misreadings: The Milgram experiment did not show that people are naturally cruel; it showed that many will obey an authority even against their conscience, a situational rather than dispositional finding. The sixty-five percent figure is not a fixed universal rate but the result of one baseline condition, with obedience varying greatly across the many variants. And the study is not a clean, settled demonstration, since its ethics and its archival record are seriously questioned, so treating it as proof of innate cruelty, as a single fixed rate, or as unimpeachable science misreads an ethically fraught and contested experiment on obedience to authority.
origin: A series of obedience-to-authority experiments conducted by the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram beginning in 1961, first published in 1963, motivated by the Eichmann trial and the psychology of the Holocaust.
